We congratulate the Evening Telegram

We congratulate the Evening Telegram on its Bar Mitzvah. Contribute to the Jewish Children's Free Excursions. ' a? 4 One Alliance is enough ! Will the U. A. H. C. start it ? f Why cannot the Jewish Publication Society be revived ? One of the most difficult problems of modern times : To find who is to blame for an accident. We are pleased to state'that the “Translations from the Talmud,” which we have intermitted for some weeks, .again grace our columns. What with steamboat accidents, rifle match, the intense heat with its accompanying death list, car strikes and explosions, the average American has had his full share of excitement and nervous' strain during the past week. There are thirty students in the New York Theological School, and thirty more' in that of Cincinnati. We' hope that in ■ due time there may be found sixty valuable positions for them all,in influential and enlightened congregations. How many of the three hundred and fifty graduates of the Normal College will : be able to obtain positions in the public ■ schools ? The Commissioners should be ' gallant enough to cause the erection of 1 new buildings in order to accommodate 1 the young ladies ! : \\ j OUR young lady coreligionists of the I Normal College deserve to be congratula- ; ted for their proficiency and for the very ; laudable desire not to be outdone by the ]

young gentlemen of their race in intellectual activity. The Jewish intellect, whether male or female, has again proven its supremacy. The Union of American Hebrew Con- । gregations has demonstrated its great usefulness, and the examinations of the College and the branches under its control, must convince the most dubious of its grand utility and importance. Every Jewish congregation in the land should join the Union! We call the.attention of our readers to the editorial reprinted in our columns from The Sun, entitled, “»What Jews are doing in our Times ?” And yet although the facts embodied in this article have been oft repeated by the liberal press is it not strange that so much prejudice should still exist against our race ? After our editorial, “ Fresh Air for the Young Ones,” was in type, we received information that a donation of two hundred and fifty dollars had also been received from a gentleman of whose benevolence । we have had many evidences, and that the Young Ladies’ Dramatic Union, a society with but a single equal in this city, has also donated four hundred and sixty-two dollars to the good cause, making a fund of over twelve htindred dollars. The wonders'of the last representation of the Passion play are now being learnt. Tableaux vivants precede each act. Adam and Eve were turned out of Eden while lambs evidently from a toy warehouse gambolled around them. The fall of the manna in the wilderness was illustrated by a rain of bits of paper; some of the manna remained during other scenes and flirted with the wind in a manner most unmannerly. At the sacrifice of Isaac there I was a ram ready, also evidently from a toy store, while the crossing of the Red Sea was represented with waves painted I in such atrocious style that it was clear that although the artist was “all at sea” ’be was certainly without a notion what an ocean is like. : ; There is an old saying that it is safe I to go to sea after an accident, because ' then greater vigilance is exercised. But [the faith of believers in this theory must be pretty well shaken by this time. Scarcely have we got over the excitement of one disaster than we are shocked by another : and we can hardly draw breath before the terrible fate of another vessel and her passengers is brought to our ears ! There are few deaths more terrible than that met on board a vessel within sight, nay alongside I a city , and in broad daylight. Until the accident on the Sound, we had enjoyed a long immunity from disasters at sea, and [

it would seem . tjlat this otr^wte old adage that it never • tn u»S\\5irf*it pours. May we have anothq&YjwrlWi of accidents for many, malhv^trfs: Our readers will find in thfs number an extract from The Churchman which gives in a nutshell the stumbling block to much practical charity ; the dislike of even the poorest people to leave their homes and kindred for the best charitable institution, if but for a short time. We may say that the Sanitarium committee have found this to be so, to so great an extent , that they will likely be compelled to abandon their proposed plan of a Sanitariumat the beach to which they intended sending weekly a number of mothers and unwell children who were to remain a few days at a time. For the present they will take out small parties on occasional (x’iirsions to Staten Island, Rockaway, Fort Lee, and other places within easy access, so as to enable mothers to reach their homes early in the evening. The Jewish Tribune says : ‘The American Hebrew has a novel idea! It suggests the formation of a stock company for the erection of tenement houses for the Jewish poor in New York. Will this journal be pleased to have a Judengasse ia the great Metropolis of America”. The American Hebrew doesnot claim the authorship of the idea, although it heartily endorses it. The idea was recent- \\ ly suggested at the meeting of the United Hebrew Charities. In answer to the ques- > tion asked us by our contemporary we would say that The American Hebrew, desirous of averting the formation of Judengassen that are being gradually developed in certain quarters of the lower part of our city, earnestly advocates a scheme by which the tendency to Judengassen can be checked. By all means give our Jewish residents, cheap, healthy, decent homes! We are informed that the Phi Beta Kappa Society, of one of our city colleges, which we had always respected for its liberality and from which we least expect-. ed religious prejudice, has recently rejected two coreligionists, who graduated from V that institution with the highest honors. ’ As Jewish graduates have heretofore frequently been rejected from this sacred(?) Greek letter organization, the underlying reason must be obvious to the dullest. When ignorant boors, whether hotel keepers or not, display narrow mindedness, we deem it undeserving of notice, but when cultured, educated gentlemen allow themselves to be controlled by the same mediaeval spirit, we deem it proper to call genj eral attention to the matter, so that our statisticians may know that educational : systems do not necessarily accomplish | what they seemingly were intended for.
